result.source_concept: Head Chef coordinating a restaurant kitchen

mappings.evidence: CPU is the Head Chef of a Computer's Kitchen.
The sous chef (Control Unit) who reads the order tickets, decides what needs to be done, and directs other kitchen staff.
The line cook (Arithmetic Logic Unit) who performs the actual cooking operations.

mappings.evidence: Sends the finished dish out to customers (output).

result.process_summary: Both the head chef and the CPU receive a set of instructions (order tickets/commands), decode them, coordinate subordinate agents (sous chef/Control Unit and line cook/ALU), perform data transformations (select ingredients/perform calculations), make logical decisions (cooking time/temperature or branching), and deliver a final product (finished dish/output). The shared causal structure is a central controller that interprets instructions, orchestrates subordinate components, and produces an output.
potential_breaks: The chef is portrayed as a single decision-maker, whereas modern CPUs have multiple cores and can execute many instructions in parallel.
Cooking involves physical, time‑consuming transformations, which differ from the near‑instantaneous electronic operations of a CPU.
The kitchen hierarchy simplifies the complex micro‑architectural mechanisms (pipelines, registers, caches) that exist inside a CPU.
The analogy treats the CPU as a sole coordinator, overlooking the distributed nature of control signals and concurrent data paths within the chip.
